Captured in Linear, and the harness is built and verified.

## Linear

**Project:** [Agentic Memory Recall](https://linear.app/muddybootscode/project/agentic-memory-recall-d00d8ddf0192) (team MUD, started, you as lead) — none existed, so I created it.

**Document:** [Memory recall: baseline measurement and root cause](https://linear.app/muddybootscode/document/memory-recall-baseline-measurement-and-root-cause-84aea9b5ad03) — the full write-up: the 11.9% baseline, the extraction root cause, the retrieval findings, the two methodology mistakes worth not repeating, and the correction to my wrong claim about identifiers.

**Issues**, all on the project:

| | |
|---|---|
| MUD-386 | Retune threshold to 0.38 and document its calibration |
| MUD-387 | Evaluate restricting recall to preferences only |
| MUD-388 | Give `ExtractedEntity` a description and embed it |
| MUD-389 | Run the extractor variant sweep |
| MUD-390 | Wire the BAML Collector for per-call visibility |
| MUD-391 | Fix duplicate entity nodes |
| MUD-392 | Stop `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` implicitly switching the embedder |

## Harness state

Six variants now run through a real `BamlRuntime` built from mutated `baml_src/extraction.baml` text. Verified: `production` renders a prompt **byte-identical** to the shipped client, and every variant differs on exactly one axis. Stripping the 18 `EntityType` annotations cuts the rendered prompt from 5809 to 4092 chars — those annotations are 30% of the prompt, which is why running them at zero invalidated the earlier control.

Traces land in `results/traces/<variant>.jsonl` with rendered prompt, raw response, usage, timing and retry attempts.

## Two bugs the design pass caught in what I'd just written

**Silent failure.** `rt.call_function` returns a *failed* `FunctionResult` rather than raising. My code only caught exceptions, so a provider outage would have become an empty extraction counted as success — quietly deflating whichever variant got unlucky. Now checked via `result.is_ok()`.

**Context manager singleton.** `BamlCtxManager.__new__` returns the pre-existing instance if one exists, and `__init__` copies its runtime. Since I import `baml_client`, my "per-variant" context was silently production's. Now minted from each variant's own runtime via `rt.create_context_manager()`.

Neither would have thrown. Both would have produced plausible, wrong numbers.

One correction to the plan's budget: at ~100 chunks × 6 variants plus 200 queries × 6, this is ~$68 at opus-5 throughout, not $50. Moving the judge to sonnet-5 brings it to ~$54; dropping to 80 chunks lands ~$45. Say which and I'll start the sweep.

items.text:
My probe was a smoke test. It was good enough to answer "is MiniLM leaving something on the table" — yes, clearly — and not good enough to choose between close candidates. Here's what a real evaluation looks like.

## M1 — Evaluate on your own corpus, at its real size

The single biggest gap. Ranking first out of 30 facts is a different task from ranking first out of 5,000. Distractors are what make retrieval hard, and I had almost none.

Use the actual graph. If it's small today, pad it with realistic distractors rather than testing on a toy. Public benchmarks like MTEB and BEIR are for **shortlisting** — narrow to 3–4 candidates — never for the final pick. Leaderboard rank routinely fails to predict domain performance, and MTEB in particular has models tuned against it.

## M2 — Get queries you didn't write

I authored both the questions and the answer key, so my sense of a "fair" question is baked into the result. Real sources, roughly in order of cost:

- **Your actual prompts.** You run a UserPromptSubmit hook and Cognee captures session traces. You have a log of real prompts. That's the true query distribution, free, and impossible to bias.
- **LLM-generated queries from your facts.** Cheap and scalable, but inherits the generator's phrasing habits. Better than hand-writing, worse than real traffic.
- **Real traffic is strictly better.** Use it if you have 100+ prompts stored.

## M3 — Get relevance labels you didn't write either

For each (query, fact) pair, someone has to say relevant or not. Options:

- **LLM-as-judge** — a strong model rates each pair. Standard practice, scales, and removes your authoring bias. Validate it once against ~50 human-labeled pairs to check agreement before trusting it at scale.
- **Human labels** on a sample — gold standard, expensive, worth it for a validation set.

**Then pool.** This is the part people skip and it matters: run every candidate model, take each one's top-k, and judge the *union*. If you only label what one model retrieved, every other model gets punished for finding relevant things your labeler never saw. Pooling is how TREC has done this for thirty years and it's the difference between a fair comparison and confirming your incumbent.

## M4 — Measure at your operating point, not top-k

This is the one specific to your system, and it's where my probe was structurally wrong for you.

Your hook doesn't take the top 5. It takes **everything above a similarity threshold**. So rank-based metrics like MRR are measuring something your code doesn't do. What you need is a **threshold sweep**: for each candidate threshold from 0.0 to 1.0, compute precision (what fraction of what you injected was relevant) and recall (what fraction of the relevant facts you injected). Plot it. Pick the threshold off the curve.

That gives you three things at once — the right model, the right threshold for that model, and the actual cost of being wrong about either. It turns F14 from a warning into a number.

Also measure what happens on queries with **no** relevant memory, which is most prompts. Precision at your threshold on those is what determines how much junk you inject into every unrelated conversation.

## M5 — Enough queries, and paired tests

Fifty queries for rough signal, 100–300 for comparisons you'd act on. Twelve is a smoke test.

Because every model sees the same queries, use **paired** significance tests — a paired bootstrap or paired t-test over per-query scores. Paired tests are far more powerful than comparing two averages, which is what lets you get away with 100 queries instead of 1,000. Report a confidence interval, not just a point estimate. If the interval crosses zero, you learned the models are indistinguishable, which is a real result.

## M6 — Don't tune and report on the same queries

Split your set. Pick the threshold on one half, report performance on the other. Otherwise you're reporting the best case you searched for, which is how a model that looked great in evaluation disappoints in production.

## M7 — Retrieval metrics are a proxy; close the loop

What you actually care about is whether injected memory improves the assistant's answers. Retrieval quality is the fast inner loop, but the ground truth is downstream: run the same task set with hook-on vs hook-off, and model A vs model B, and judge answer quality. It's slower and noisier, and it's the only measurement that reflects the thing you're building.

## Concretely, for this project

Stage 1 is maybe a day's work and would settle the model choice properly: harvest 150 real prompts from your session history, embed the real graph, LLM-judge the pooled top-10 from MiniLM, bge-base, and voyage-4, then sweep the threshold for each.

The threshold sweep alone is worth doing regardless of which model you pick, since it's the thing your code has a hardcoded guess for.

Want me to build that harness? It reuses the scripts in the scratchpad. The part I'd need from you is where the real prompt history lives.

Pushed `7eedacd` (F6) and `cd3af5b` (F7).

## F1

The mechanism, concretely. `anthropic_enabled()` is just "key is present and non-empty" (`providers.py:40`). It drives three things at once:

1. `default_baml_options()` — extraction routes to Anthropic instead of the Resilient/Bedrock chain.
2. `embedding_kwargs_from_env()` — the embedder default flips from `bedrock`/1024 to `sentence_transformers`/384.
3. `server.py:96` — the whole credential preflight returns early, so nothing checks anything at startup.

Only #2 causes damage. Extraction moving to Anthropic is a spend and model surprise, recoverable. Embeddings dropping to 384 against a graph whose `*_embedding_idx` were built at 1024 either fails every vector query or, once an index is recreated, leaves mixed-dimension vectors and silently degraded recall. The README already carries the "use a fresh graph" warning, so the hazard is known — it's just unenforced, and the trigger is an env var many people have exported globally for unrelated reasons.

There is no dimension check anywhere in the codebase (`grep -rn dimension src` finds only the config values).

**O1 — gate everything on explicit `NAM_LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic`.** The key alone does nothing. Compose sets the variable in `docker-compose.yml`, so `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... docker compose up -d` keeps its one-variable ergonomics; only host-side runs have to opt in. Coherent, and the accidental path disappears.

**O2 — keep implicit activation, add a startup guard.** Read the existing `*_embedding_idx` dimensions from Neo4j, compare against the configured embedder, refuse to start on mismatch. This catches the F3 path and hand-rolled misconfiguration too, not just this trigger. It doesn't address the "my extraction silently moved providers" surprise.

**O3 — split the two.** Key activates Anthropic extraction only; embeddings never switch implicitly. Precise, but it breaks the PR's premise: key-only mode would still reach for Bedrock embeddings and need AWS credentials, so "no Bedrock at all" stops being true.

I'd do O1 with O2 behind it. O1 removes the accident, O2 catches every other route to the same corruption, and compose absorbs the ergonomic cost so the documented happy path is unchanged. O3 looks like the surgical option but costs you the feature.

items.text:
No first-party Anthropic embeddings model or API exists. Never has. Claude generates text; Anthropic deliberately skipped the embeddings market as commoditized and low-differentiation. Their own docs have an "Embeddings" page whose content is a recommendation to use **Voyage AI**, plus a cookbook for it.

So the situation across your three provider paths:

- **Bedrock** — Titan embeddings, 1024. Already wired.
- **OpenAI** — `text-embedding-3-small`/`-large`. Already wired: the `openai` extra is in your pinned dependency and `_embedder_patch.py` has the branch.
- **Anthropic** — nothing. The key buys you extraction only, which is exactly why `providers.py:85` has to guess at an embedder.

That guess is the whole of F1. It isn't a bug in the sense of someone forgetting a branch — there is no branch to write.

Two notes on Voyage, since Anthropic points there. `voyage-3-large` tops MTEB and supports `output_dimension` of 1024, so it would slot into a Titan-built index schema. But it's a hosted API with its own key, so it reintroduces a second vendor and per-query network latency into a hook with a 5s budget — and upstream has no Voyage provider, so it'd need a third patch alongside the Bedrock one. For local compose mode, the point of which is "one key, no cloud dependencies," a local model is still the right answer.

None of this changes O10. `bge-base-en-v1.5` remains the recommendation.

Sources: [Anthropic — Embeddings](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/embeddings), [anthropics/claude-cookbooks — VoyageAI](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-cookbooks/blob/main/third_party/VoyageAI/how_to_create_embeddings.md)

Page and both write-ups updated: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/82f845e8-2ccb-45e0-9f1b-922138cb7d22 · MUD-394

items.text:
Researched. One finding reframes the question, so I'll lead with it.

## F8 — you cannot match Titan, only its dimension count

Embeddings from two different models live in different coordinate spaces. A vector from `bge-large` and a vector from Titan can both be 1024 numbers long and still be completely incomparable — cosine similarity between them is noise, not a weak signal. So "match Titan" isn't available at any model choice. Any provider switch means re-embedding every node in the graph.

Matching 1024 dims buys exactly one thing: the Neo4j index schema doesn't have to be dropped and recreated. That's it.

## F9 — a 1024-dim local model makes F1 worse, not better

Right now the accidental provider switch fails loudly: 384-dim vectors hit a 1024-dim index and every vector query errors. If we move local embeddings to 1024, that guard disappears. An exported `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` would silently write incomparable vectors into a Titan-built graph and searches would just quietly return wrong results.

So if you want a 1024 local model, O1 or O2 from the F1 discussion stops being optional.

## F10 — the upstream embedder limits which models are usable

Three constraints in `neo4j_agent_memory/embeddings/sentence_transformers.py`:

1. `SentenceTransformerEmbedder(model_name, device)` — no `truncate_dim`, so Matryoshka truncation isn't reachable without another patch alongside the Bedrock one.
2. `model.encode(text)` is called with no `prompt_name`. Models trained with mandatory query prefixes — E5 (`query:` / `passage:`), BGE (`Represent this sentence for searching...`) — run degraded. This rules out the naive drop-in for most of the leaderboard.
3. The `dimensions` property falls back to `MODEL_DIMENSIONS.get(name, 384)` for any model it doesn't know. The index is built from `NAM_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS` instead, so setting the model without the dimension gives you a 384 index holding 1024 vectors. Same family of footgun as F1.

## Candidates

| Model | Params | Dims | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (current) | 22M | 384 | 2022-era. 78.1% top-5 on TREC-COVID. ~256 token limit. No prefix needed. |
| `bge-base-en-v1.5` | 110M | 768 | 84.7% top-5. Wants a query prefix we can't send. |
| `embeddinggemma-300m` | 300M | 768 | Built for on-device, ~50ms CPU. Uses task prompts we can't send. |
| `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` | 600M | **1024** | Top open-weight at this size. Instruction optional — only 1–5% loss without it. 32k context. |

**O8 — `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B`.** It's the only strong candidate whose quality doesn't depend on the prefix support we lack, and its native 1024 leaves the index schema alone. The open question is CPU latency: 600M params against MiniLM's 22M, inside a container, under the recall hook's 5s budget and the ~400ms warm search the README advertises.

**O9 — `bge-base-en-v1.5` at 768.** Materially better than MiniLM, 5x the parameters instead of 27x, but a new index dimension and a known-degraded query path.

I'd measure before choosing. I can benchmark MiniLM, bge-base, and Qwen3-0.6B on this machine for cold load, warm single-query latency, and batch throughput — that turns O8 vs O9 into a number rather than a blog claim. Want me to run it?

Sources: [Presenc AI open-weight roundup](https://presenc.ai/research/best-open-weight-embedding-models-2026), [Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), [google/embeddinggemma-300m](https://huggingface.co/google/embeddinggemma-300m), [Supermemory benchmark](https://supermemory.ai/blog/best-open-source-embedding-models-benchmarked-and-ranked/), [Milvus 2026 comparison](https://milvus.io/blog/choose-embedding-model-rag-2026.md)
